extracted.intended_audience: Academic researchers/applicants to NSF grants (PIs, postdocs, faculty writing proposals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for understanding NSF panel ratings and what different priority categories mean for funding chances, plus practical advice for reading panel summaries and preparing resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority categories (high / medium / low / not competitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF does not use a numerical score/cut-off but instead places proposals in one of four categories: high, medium, low priority, and not competitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categorical rankings are the primary signal of relative merit from the panel. Being in the top three categories means the panel considered your ideas worthwhile; being 'not competitive' is roughly equivalent to triage. There is no internal numeric ordering within each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context statement / program-wide proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The context statement tells you how many proposals came into that program and what percentage were placed in each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these percentages to understand how selective the panel/program was (examples given range from ~5% to ~55% in the 'not competitive' bin). This gives insight into both your competition and how the panel tends to grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'not competitive'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Not competitive' signals a proposal flaw perceived as large enough that the panel would not trust the project to produce results worthy of funding, even with abundant resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If placed here, the panel summary should explain the reasons; read summaries carefully because many are not blunt. Treat this as a signal you need substantial revision to be fundable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the panel summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel summary often contains the clearest, most actionable information about strengths and weaknesses and is worth starting with when reading reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the issues raised in the panel summary in revisions. Sometimes you must 'read between the lines' because summaries can be understated; a good panel summary contains a lot of useful information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio and Program Officer (PO) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: After panel ranking, POs make funding decisions based on portfolio needs — e.g., ensuring PUI participation, EPSCoR considerations, career-stage balance, and other programmatic goals (such as OPUS-type projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even highly-ranked proposals can be passed over if they don't help the PO meet portfolio constraints, and lower-ranked proposals in desirable categories (e.g., from EPSCoR states or early-career investigators) may be funded to meet mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-three categories are technically fundable
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything placed in the high, medium, or low priority categories is technically eligible for funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because POs have leeway and there is no within-category ranking, being in one of the top three categories is often more important than being 'high' versus 'medium' — medium-ranked proposals can receive funding if budget and portfolio needs allow; conversely, high-ranked proposals can still go unfunded.

rubrics_metrics.name: No within-category ranking / lack of numeric precision
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF's categorical scheme does not provide a numeric ordering inside each category, unlike continuous scoring systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of granularity gives PO discretion and means that small differences in perceived merit may not translate directly to funding likelihood; interpret category placement with that in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel judgments are context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are judged in the context of what else is on the table in a given review round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposal that was highly ranked in one round may fare worse in another if the competition is stronger or the panel's composition/goals differ. Panel discussions compare proposals against each other, not against an absolute standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission strategy: address previous concerns without creating new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising after a decline, change enough to resolve prior criticisms but avoid making changes that invite new concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels resent seeing proposals recycled into the next round without addressing earlier issues. Strategic, targeted revisions that close identified gaps are preferable to large overhauls that may introduce fresh weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation across panels/programs in wording and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different NSF programs or panels sometimes use different rating language or internal processes (terminology used on panels may not match panel summaries seen by PIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform review language or procedures across programs. If your panel or program used different terminology, focus on the substance of criticisms rather than exact phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review triage and uneven feedback practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Some panels may discard a large fraction of proposals before full discussion (resulting in no feedback), while other panels review all submissions and provide comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your proposal is thrown out in an initial cut, you may receive no feedback, which complicates improvement. Expect variability and, when feedback is given, use it carefully to guide revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and external budget uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Time from panel meeting to PO contact varies (examples 4–6 months); external factors like congressional budgets can delay PO decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume a fixed turnaround; POs may hold decisions to see if additional funds become available, particularly for proposals near funding cutoffs.
